summaries.example: Imagine a class sorting objects. A red ball and a red book are different things, but they share redness. Burley asked whether shared features, such as being human or being red, are real features in the world or only ideas in our minds. He thought shared natures mattered for explaining how words and knowledge work.
summaries.summary: Walter Burley was a major philosopher of the fourteenth century. He studied at Oxford and Paris, taught, took part in academic debates, and wrote about fifty works. Much of his philosophy discussed Aristotle’s logic and studies of nature. A central question was whether general features, called universals, are real. Early on, Burley held a moderate form of realism: common natures exist in individual things, while the mind also forms concepts of them. Later, after engaging with William of Ockham’s arguments, he defended a more extreme realism. He said universals, individuals, categories, and true states of affairs have distinct kinds of reality. Burley also connected meaning with reality. General words refer to many individuals through the common nature they signify, and true sentences correspond to how things are. His account of knowledge changed too. In one period, the intellect mainly knows universals directly and individuals indirectly. Later, he argued that the intellect first knows singular things and reaches universals through abstraction and reflection.
key_ideas: Walter Burley was an important fourteenth-century philosopher who taught and wrote in England and France.
He wrote many works about logic, nature, knowledge, and Aristotle’s philosophy.
Early in his career, he said universals exist in individual things and also as ideas in the mind.
Later, he defended a stronger realism: universals and individual things are really different, though connected.
He thought true sentences must match how things are in the world.
His views changed partly because he was responding to William of Ockham’s criticisms.
summaries.why_it_matters: Burley helps us see that questions about language are also questions about reality. When we use a general word such as “horse,” are we pointing only to many separate horses, or also to a shared nature? His changing answers show how philosophers revise theories when they meet difficult objections. His work also connects three important subjects: what exists, how words mean, and how people know things.

important_terms.definition: A feature or nature that can belong to many individual things, such as humanity shared by many people.
The study of what exists and what kinds of things there are.
The study of how words, sentences, and thoughts mean things.
A view that says common features are real in some way, not merely names we invent.

questions_to_think_about: Is redness something real in red objects, or only a word we use for them?
Can we know a particular object before we understand the general kind it belongs to?
Why might a philosopher change an opinion after hearing a strong criticism?

summaries.example: Consider the sentence “Socrates is a human.” Burley’s later theory distinguishes the individual Socrates from the universal humanity, so they are not numerically the same entity. Yet the sentence can be true because the term “human” has personal supposition for Socrates: the individual named by the subject is among the things that instantiate the universal. The sentence therefore expresses a real relation in the world while preserving a distinction between the universal and its instance.
summaries.summary: Walter Burley was one of the most influential philosophers of the fourteenth century. His surviving works include commentaries and treatises on logic, Aristotle’s Physics, psychology, ethics, politics, categories, and universals. The SEP entry emphasizes the development of his views rather than presenting a single unchanging system. In his earlier ontology, only substance, quantity, and quality are fully real entities; other categories are real aspects grounded in them. Universals exist as common natures in individuals and as concepts in the mind, but their being is not independent of their instances. His semantics links terms to their significata. Abstract terms signify forms, general terms signify universals, and concrete accidental terms signify aggregates of substance and accidental form. True propositions correspond to the way things are, though Burley’s early account gives real propositions an unstable status as objects of thought. After 1324, in response to Ockham’s critique of traditional realism, Burley developed a stronger ontology. Macro-objects are ordered aggregates of primary substances and substantial and accidental forms. Universals are really distinct from individuals, and the ten categories are really distinct from one another. His later semantics separates a sentence’s mental content from the real proposition or state of affairs that can make it true. Burley’s theory of knowledge also shifts: his earlier account gives the universal priority for intellective cognition, while his later account treats singulars as the first objects of confused intellectual knowledge and universals as reached through abstraction and reflection.
key_ideas: Burley’s career produced two related semantic systems connected to two different accounts of reality.
His early moderate realism held that universals exist in individuals as common natures and also exist mentally as concepts; their being does not exceed the being of their instances.
His later ontology introduced real distinctions among universals and individuals, among the Aristotelian categories, and between simple objects and complex states of affairs.
Burley treated logic as grounded in metaphysics: the structure of valid discourse should correspond to structural features of reality.
His semantics distinguishes sense from significatum, and in the later theory gives false sentences a mental content even when no matching state of affairs exists.
His epistemology changed from treating the universal as the intellect’s direct object to treating singulars as known first in confused cognition, with universals reached by abstraction.
summaries.why_it_matters: Burley is important because his work joins issues that are often studied separately: universals, categories, reference, truth, and cognition. His response to Ockham shows one way a realist might try to preserve knowledge of an external world without retaining the earlier identity between universals and particulars. The disagreements among interpreters about whether Burley had one evolving theory or several also show why historical philosophy requires careful attention to terminology, chronology, and the relation between different texts.

important_terms.definition: A common nature or form that can be present in, and predicated of, many individuals.
A theory of what exists and how entities are structured; Burley developed different ontologies during his career.
The study of meaning, including what expressions signify and what they stand for in context.
A realist position that treats universals as having some reality beyond merely being names or concepts.
The distinction between a term’s essential content and the individuals to which it applies.
A medieval semantic theory concerning what a term stands for in a proposition, either a common nature or individual instances.
A complex object or state of affairs that, in Burley’s later view, can make a true sentence true.
A philosophical view associated here with Burley’s later realism, in which universals and individuals are really distinct.

questions_to_think_about: Does a distinction between a universal and its instances solve the problems raised against moderate realism, or create new ones?
Can a false sentence have meaning if nothing in reality makes it true?
Should the meaning of a general term be explained by its mental concept, its real universal, its instances, or all of these?
Why would a theory of knowledge need to explain both singular cognition and universal concepts?
What does Burley’s changing view suggest about the relationship between logic and metaphysics?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “That animal is a horse.” The animal is one particular thing, while “horse” is a general word that can apply to many animals. Burley’s later view says the particular animal and the universal horse-nature are really distinct, but the universal is present in the individual and helps explain why the word “horse” applies. A true sentence works because the word and the thing it describes fit the way reality is organized.
summaries.summary: Walter Burley was a prominent philosopher of the fourteenth century. He studied and taught at Oxford and Paris, participated in academic debates, and wrote about fifty works, many of which circulated widely. The SEP entry focuses on how his thinking developed. Early in his career, Burley defended moderate realism. On this view, universals are common natures found in individual things, and the mind also forms concepts of them. He analyzed language by asking what words signify. A general term such as “human” can apply to many people because it signifies a common nature, while a proper name refers to one individual. He also distinguished a term’s intension from its extension: roughly, its content from the things to which it applies. Burley’s account of truth connected language and reality. A true sentence must correspond to how things are, although his early explanation of the state of affairs signified by a sentence faced difficulties, especially for false sentences. Later, partly in response to William of Ockham, Burley developed a stronger form of realism. He described the world as containing individual substances, universal forms, accidental forms, distinct categories, and complex states of affairs. This allowed him to explain false sentences as meaningful mental constructions even when no matching state of affairs exists. His theory of knowledge also changed. Earlier, the intellect directly understood universals and reached individuals indirectly. Later, he argued that singular things are known first in confused cognition, while universals are obtained through abstraction and reflection. For more organized knowledge, however, we use general concepts and definitions to explain a thing’s structure.
key_ideas: Burley was a widely read medieval philosopher who wrote about logic, metaphysics, nature, psychology, ethics, and politics.
His early position was a moderate realism: universals exist in individual things as common natures and also appear in the mind as concepts.
His later position became more radical. Universals and individuals were then treated as really distinct parts or features of the world.
Burley believed language should be explained by examining reality, but he also thought our account of reality should help solve problems about language.
He held that truth involves a fit between a sentence, thought, and the way things are.
His account of knowledge changed: early writings give universals a direct role for the intellect, while later writings give priority to singular things in the development of knowledge.
summaries.why_it_matters: Burley’s philosophy matters because it shows how a debate about general words can affect theories of reality, truth, and knowledge. His exchange with Ockham illustrates that medieval philosophers were carefully testing rival explanations, not simply repeating inherited ideas. Studying Burley also helps us understand why philosophers distinguish individual objects, common kinds, mental concepts, and the states of affairs described by sentences.

important_terms.definition: A common nature that can belong to many individual things, such as the nature shared by different horses.
A philosophical account of what exists and how different kinds of things are related.
The study of how words and sentences get their meanings and connect with things.
The view that universals have some real status, rather than being only names made by people.
What a word means or conveys, compared with the things it applies to.
A rule about what a term stands for in a particular sentence or argument.
A complex state of affairs that can be what a true sentence describes.

questions_to_think_about: Are general ideas like “human” and “triangle” real features, mental ideas, or just words?
Why might Ockham’s criticisms lead Burley to strengthen rather than abandon realism?
How can a sentence be meaningful even when it is false?
Is it easier to learn about a particular object first or about its general category first?
Should logic describe the structure of language, the structure of reality, or both?
